questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presented with a 5-day history of fevers and rash and a 2-day history of swelling of the hands and feet. He had received all childhood vaccinations. He had no recent foreign travel and no sick contacts. He did not attend nursery and was a single child. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C, he had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, and a macular perineal rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kawasaki syndrome Measles is less likely in a vaccinated child. Rubella and parvovirus infection do not involve conjunctiva. SJS would progress with more extensive cutaneous disease. Kawasaki disease typically presents with the above features.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q46

questions.question: Kawasaki question – 8 yo kid with 5 day fever and polymorphic rash, N/V, conjunctivitis. ESR 85, WBC 12, Plts 330

parts.text: What are 4 other infections to consider

questions.model_answer:
a) Four major (classic) criteria of KD (aside from fever ≥5 days), any 4 of: (1) bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, (2) oral mucosal changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, oropharyngeal erythema), (3) polymorphous rash, (4) changes in the extremities (erythema/edema of hands and feet acutely, periungual desquamation later), (5) cervical lymphadenopathy (usually unilateral, >1.5 cm) — pick 4 of these 5.
b) Infections to consider in differential: (1) adenovirus, (2) enterovirus, (3) measles, (4) staphylococcal or streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (also parvovirus, scarlet fever, leptospirosis).
c) Two other clinical features of KD: (1) noncalculous cholecystitis/gallbladder hydrops, (2) arthritis/arthralgia (also aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, sterile pyuria).
d) Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion plus high-dose aspirin, given within the first 10 days of fever onset (ideally to reduce coronary aneurysm risk); transition aspirin to low antiplatelet dose after fever resolves.

questions.question: 6-year-old boy has fever for 5 days, then presents to medical attention with a pleomorphic rash, pharyngitis, strawberry tongue and elevated inflammatory markers. You suspect Kawasaki's disease – (2019)

parts.text: A) Other than fever, what are four diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki's disease?
B) What are 4 infectious aetiologies that should be excluded?
C) What are 2 serious complications that can arise from Kawasaki's disease?
D) What are 2 medical therapies that are used in the treatment of this condition

cohort_answer.text: Diagnostic criteria: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection; Oral mucous membrane changes (fissured lips, injected pharynx, strawberry tongue); Erythema of palms and soles or periungal desquamation; Polymorphous rash; Cervical lymphadenopathy. Infectious etiologies to exclude: Adenovirus; Measles; EBV; Echovirus. Complications: Coronary artery aneurysm; MI. Therapies: IVIG; Aspirin; Glucocorticoids

parts.text: Other than fever, name major criteria

cohort_answer.text: Major criteria: cervical lymphadenopathy (often unilateral), strawberry tongue/buccal mucosa, non-purulent conjunctivitis, macular rash/rash on hands that desquamates (CREAM-F: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Extremity/Adenopathy, Mucosal changes, Fever). Infectious DDx: Toxic Shock (strep or staph), Measles, Adenovirus, EBV, RMSF, COVID MIS-C. Complications: coronary artery aneurysms, MI. Treatments: IVIG, ASA; if not improving, steroids and biologics (infliximab). Diagnosis requires 5 of 6 criteria including fever; incomplete Kawasaki if fever ≥5 days and 2-3 other manifestations.

questions.question: You see a 9 month-old child presenting with fever, irritability, and hypotension. They have a diffuse erythematous rash involving the face, trunk, and extremities, with regions of desquamation and bull formation. The lips are cracked but there is no oral involvement. Application of pressure adjacent to a bulla leads to it rupturing.

parts.text: What is the name of the most likely condition?
What is the toxin responsible for this condition?
MIS-C is also on the differentiation diagnosis. Name TWO organ systems and ONE finding in each system that are on the WHO diagnostic criteria.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely condition: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS).
b) Toxin responsible: toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) (a superantigen).
c) MIS-C WHO diagnostic criteria - 2 organ systems and 1 finding in each: (1) Cardiovascular - hypotension or shock (or evidence of myocardial dysfunction, e.g., elevated troponin/BNP, pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities); (2) Gastrointestinal - abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea.
questions.beyond_mandell: WHO/CDC MIS-C case definition criteria are not covered in this Mandell Staph aureus chapter.

questions.question: 8 month old child with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, irritability. Has cracked lips, no other oral involvement. No conjunctivitis. Confluent erythematous rash over face, trunk, and diaper region. Positive Nikolsky sign.

parts.text: What toxin is responsible for this (0.5)
MIS-C is on the differential for this patient. Name two organ systems involved and one symptom/manifestation for each that would meet the WHO criteria (2)

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Toxin: Exfoliative toxin A and B. MIS-C organ systems: Cardiac - pericarditis or cardiac dysfunction on echo; GI - diarrhea, nausea, vomiting; Integumentary - rash/mucocutaneous inflammation of hands/feet
